decks.title: Sets — Part 1: Sets, subsets and intervals
goals: Decide when a collection is a set and write it in roster and set-builder form
Classify sets as empty, singleton, finite, infinite or equal
Find subsets and the power set of a finite set
Use the universal set and write intervals of real numbers

slides.heading: Sets, Part 1: Collections with a clear rule
slides.body_md: A set is a collection whose membership is settled by a clear rule.

visual.alt: Table of four collections. Prime numbers below 20 and the vowels of the English alphabet are well defined sets with listed elements; tall students and good songs are not, because no clear rule decides membership.
visual.caption: A set needs a rule that settles membership.

slides.narration: Welcome to Class Eleven mathematics. Everything in this course is built on sets. A set is a collection of objects with a clear rule that decides whether any object belongs. The prime numbers below twenty form a set. The tall students of a class do not, because tall has no exact meaning. In this part you will write sets in two ways, classify them, and count their subsets.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Tell a **well-defined** collection from an opinion
slides.narration: Here are your goals for part one. You will learn to spot a genuine set, to write it by listing or by a rule, and to sort sets into types. Then you will study subsets, count them with a simple doubling rule, and finish with intervals, the sets of real numbers that every later chapter uses.

slides.heading: Elements and notation
slides.body_md: Objects in a set are its **elements**. We write $a \in A$ for "$a$ belongs to $A$" and $a \notin A$ otherwise. Capital letters name sets; standard sets are $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{W}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$.

visual.alt: Flow diagram of number sets, each inside the next: natural numbers inside whole numbers inside integers inside rational numbers inside real numbers.
visual.caption: Each number set is a subset of the next.

slides.narration: The objects in a set are called its elements. We say that an element belongs to the set and use a rounded e symbol for it. Capital letters name sets. Five number sets have fixed names: natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers and real numbers. Each is contained in the next, as the chain on screen shows.

slides.heading: Roster form and set-builder form
slides.body_md: **Roster form** lists the elements: $\{7, 14, 21\}$. **Set-builder form** gives a rule: $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a multiple of } 7,\ x < 22\}$. Each element is listed once; order does not matter.

rows: $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a multiple of } 7,\ x < 40\}$

visual.alt: Table converting four sets from set-builder form to roster form: multiples of 7 below 40 give 7, 14, 21, 28, 35; integers with x squared at most 10 give minus 3 to 3; divisors of 18 give six numbers; squares of 1 to 4 give 1, 4, 9, 16.
visual.caption: Same set, two ways of writing it.

slides.narration: There are two ways to write a set. Roster form lists the elements between curly brackets. Set-builder form states a rule that every element satisfies, such as multiples of seven below forty. The table converts four sets from rule to list. Notice that the integers whose square is at most ten include negative numbers as well, so check the universe you are working in.

slides.heading: Quick check: is it a set?
slides.body_md: Pick the collection that is well defined.

visual.alt: Table of four collections. Prime numbers below 20 and the vowels of the English alphabet are well defined sets with listed elements; tall students and good songs are not, because no clear rule decides membership.
visual.caption: A set needs a rule that settles membership.

slides.narration: Look for the option where a clear rule decides membership for every object.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from rule to list
slides.body_md: Write $A = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : -3 \le 2x + 1 < 9\}$ in roster form and find $n(A)$.

visual.alt: Table of the steps for the worked example: the inequality, its solution minus 2 up to but not including 4, the six integers from minus 2 to 3, and the count 6.
visual.caption: Solve, then list the integers allowed.

slides.narration: Solve the inequality like an equation. Subtract one from all three parts, then divide by two. The result says x is at least minus two and less than four. Now remember that x must be an integer, so list the integers in that range. There are six of them, so the set has six elements.

slides.heading: Types of sets
slides.body_md: **Empty** $\varnothing$: no element. **Singleton**: one element. **Finite**: counting ends. **Infinite**: it does not. Note $\{\varnothing\}$ is **not** empty; it has one element.

visual.alt: Table of types of sets with an example each: an empty set with 0 elements, a singleton with 1 element, a finite set of primes below 12 with 5 elements, and the infinite set of even natural numbers whose elements never end.
visual.caption: Count the elements to decide the type.

slides.narration: Sets are classified by their size. The empty set has no elements and is written with a slashed circle. A singleton has exactly one. A finite set can be counted to the end, while an infinite set, like the even natural numbers, never finishes. A trap to remember: a set containing the empty set has one element, so it is not itself empty.

slides.heading: Equal sets
slides.body_md: Sets $A$ and $B$ are **equal** when they have exactly the same elements. Repeating or reordering elements changes nothing. Equal sets have equal counts, but equal counts do **not** make sets equal.

visual.alt: Table testing four sets against 1, 2, 3: the same elements in another order, with repeats, or described by x below 4 are all equal to it; the set described by x at most 4 has the extra element 4 and is not equal.
visual.caption: Order and repeats do not matter; the elements do.

slides.narration: Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements. Writing the elements in another order, or repeating one, does not change the set. The table tests four descriptions against the set one, two, three. The last one has an extra element four, so it is different. Remember also that two sets may have the same number of elements without being equal.

slides.heading: Quick check: the empty set
slides.body_md: Is the set containing only the empty set itself an empty set?
slides.narration: Count the elements inside the outer brackets.

slides.heading: Subsets
slides.body_md: $B \subseteq A$ if every element of $B$ is in $A$. If also $B \ne A$, then $B$ is a **proper subset**, written $B \subset A$. The empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram inside a rectangle U of 1 to 8: a large circle A holds 1, 3, 5, 6 and, inside it, a small circle B holds 2 and 4; 7 and 8 lie outside both circles.
visual.caption: $B = \{2, 4\}$ sits inside $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$: $B \subset A$.

slides.narration: A set B is a subset of A when every element of B also lies in A. In the picture, the small circle inside the large one shows this: two and four are in both. If B is not all of A, it is a proper subset. Two facts to memorise: the empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself.

slides.heading: The power set
slides.body_md: The set of all subsets of $A$ is the **power set** $P(A)$. If $n(A) = n$, then $P(A)$ has $2^n$ elements, because each element is either in or out of a subset.

visual.alt: Table listing all 8 subsets of a, b, c by size: 1 subset of size 0, which is the empty set; 3 of size 1; 3 of size 2; and 1 of size 3, the set itself. The counts 1, 3, 3, 1 add up to 8.
visual.caption: Total $1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8 = 2^3$.

slides.narration: List every subset of the three-element set a, b, c, sorted by size. There is one with no elements, three with one element, three with two, and one with all three. That is eight subsets in all. The reason is simple: each element is either in or out, two choices each, so three elements give two times two times two.

slides.heading: Subsets double with each new element
slides.body_md: Subsets: $2^n$. Proper subsets: $2^n - 1$. Non-empty proper subsets: $2^n - 2$.

visual.alt: Table of the number of subsets of a set with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 elements: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, doubling each time.
visual.caption: Each new element doubles the number of subsets: $2^n$.

slides.narration: Here is the doubling in numbers. A set with no elements has one subset, itself. Add one element and the count doubles to two, then four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two. Remove the set itself to count proper subsets, and remove the empty set as well to count the non-empty proper ones. These three counts are the usual one-mark questions.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting with conditions
slides.body_md: How many subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ contain both $3$ and $5$?
bullets: $3$ and $5$ must be in the subset
Each of $1, 2, 4$ is free: in or out

visual.alt: Table for the worked example: elements 3 and 5 are fixed inside, one way; elements 1, 2 and 4 are free, 2 times 2 times 2 ways; the total is 8 subsets.
visual.caption: Fixed elements add no choice.

slides.narration: When some elements are forced into the subset, only the other elements give a choice. Here three and five must be inside, so there is only one way for them. The remaining elements one, two and four are each in or out, giving two cubed, which is eight subsets. Checking by listing all thirty-two subsets confirms the count.

slides.heading: Quick check: subsets of a six-element set
slides.body_md: Fill in the number of subsets of a set with six elements.
slides.narration: Use the doubling rule with six elements.

slides.heading: Universal set
slides.body_md: Within one discussion, all sets are subsets of a fixed **universal set** $U$, drawn as a rectangle. In a Venn diagram, circles inside the rectangle represent subsets.

visual.alt: A rectangle U holding the numbers 1 to 10 with one circle A containing 2, 3, 5 and 7; the remaining numbers 1, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10 lie outside the circle but inside the rectangle.
visual.caption: The universal set $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 10\}$ is the rectangle; $A$ is the circle of primes.

slides.narration: In any problem, all the sets live inside one larger set, called the universal set. We draw it as a rectangle, and draw each set as a circle inside. Here the universal set is the numbers one to ten and the circle holds the primes. The numbers left outside the circle but inside the rectangle are the ones that are not prime.

slides.heading: Intervals of real numbers
slides.body_md: Intervals are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. A **square** bracket includes the end point; a **round** bracket excludes it. Infinity $\infty$ is never included.

visual.alt: Table pairing four set-builder descriptions with their interval notation: open interval from minus 2 to 3, closed interval, half-open interval with minus 2 included, and the unbounded interval above minus 2.
visual.caption: Round bracket: excluded. Square bracket: included.

slides.narration: Sets of real numbers between two end points are called intervals. A square bracket means the end point is included, a round bracket means it is excluded. The symbol for infinity always gets a round bracket, because it is not a number. The table matches four set-builder descriptions with their interval notation.

slides.heading: Intervals on the number line
slides.body_md: Filled circle: included. Open circle: excluded. Arrow: continues for ever.

slides.narration: On the number line, each interval is a thick line. A filled circle at an end point means the point is included, and an open circle means it is excluded. An arrow means the interval never stops. The four rows show an open interval, a closed interval, a half-open interval, and one that goes on for ever to the right.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: integers in an interval
slides.body_md: How many integers lie in $(-2, 3)$, in $[-2, 3]$ and in $[-2, 3)$?

visual.alt: Table counting the integers in three intervals with end points minus 2 and 3: open gives minus 1 to 2, four integers; closed gives minus 2 to 3, six integers; left-closed right-open gives minus 2 to 2, five integers.
visual.caption: End points decide the count.

slides.narration: The end points decide the count. In the open interval both ends are removed, leaving minus one to two, four integers. In the closed interval both ends stay, giving minus two to three, six integers. The half-open interval keeps minus two but drops three, so it has five integers.

slides.heading: Quick check: integers in an interval
slides.body_md: Count the integers in a half-open interval.
slides.narration: Decide first which end point is included and which is not.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Set: well-defined collection; roster form and set-builder form
Empty, singleton, finite, infinite; equal sets have the same elements
Subset, proper subset, universal set; $\varnothing \subseteq A$ always
Number of subsets of an $n$-element set: $2^n$
Intervals: square bracket included, round bracket excluded

visual.alt: Summary flow: a set is a well-defined collection; write it in roster, set-builder or interval form; classify it as empty, finite, infinite or equal to another; subsets of an n-element set number 2 to the power n.
visual.caption: From a collection to its subsets.

slides.narration: To sum up. A set is a well-defined collection, written by listing or by a rule. Sets can be empty, finite, infinite or equal. A subset has all its elements in the larger set, and a set with n elements has two to the power n subsets. Finally, intervals are sets of real numbers, with square brackets for included ends and round brackets for excluded ends.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Roster form (1–2 marks):** solve the condition, then list every element once
**Subset counts (1–2 marks):** state $2^n$ and the reason
**Intervals (1–2 marks):** correct brackets earn the mark; wrong end point loses it
**Mistakes:** forgetting negative integers or $0$ in $\mathbb{Z}$; a square bracket next to $\infty$
**Not in this chapter:** Mathematical Induction is formative only
slides.narration: In board-style answers, marks go to the roster form with every element listed once, to the power of two count with its reason, and to correct brackets in an interval. Common slips are calling a set that holds the empty set empty, forgetting negative integers, and putting a square bracket next to infinity. One note: proof by induction is only formative and is not examined here.

decks.title: Sets — Part 2: Operations, laws and counting
goals: Find union, intersection, difference and complement from sets and Venn diagrams
Use the laws of set algebra including De Morgan
Solve word problems with the counting formulas for two and three sets

slides.heading: Sets, Part 2: Combining sets
slides.body_md: Union, intersection, difference and complement build new sets from old ones.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 10 with two overlapping circles: P holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7 and O holds the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Only P has 2; the overlap has 3, 5, 7; only O has 1 and 9; 4, 6, 8, 10 lie outside both.
visual.caption: Primes $P$ and odd numbers $O$ in $U = \{1, \dots, 10\}$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here two sets, the primes and the odd numbers up to ten, overlap in a Venn diagram. Three, five and seven are in both. You will see how to combine sets in four ways, how the laws of set algebra let you rewrite expressions, and how Venn diagrams turn word problems into simple counting.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Count with $n(A \cup B)$ and $n(A \cup B \cup C)$
slides.narration: Here are your goals for part two. You will compute the four operations from lists and diagrams, apply the laws of set algebra, combine intervals on the number line, and solve practical counting problems with the union formula for two sets, and a lighter version for three.

slides.heading: Union and intersection
slides.body_md: $A \cup B$: elements in $A$ **or** $B$ (or both). $A \cap B$: elements in **both**. If $A \cap B = \varnothing$ the sets are **disjoint**.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 10 with two overlapping circles: P holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7 and O holds the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Only P has 2; the overlap has 3, 5, 7; only O has 1 and 9; 4, 6, 8, 10 lie outside both.
visual.caption: Primes $P$ and odd numbers $O$ in $U = \{1, \dots, 10\}$.

math: A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}, \quad A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}
slides.narration: The union of two sets collects everything that is in the first, or the second, or both. The intersection keeps only what is in both. In the diagram, the union is all three regions inside the circles, and the intersection is the overlap with three, five and seven. Elements are listed once, even when they appear in both sets.

slides.heading: Disjoint sets
slides.body_md: Sets with no common element are **disjoint**: their circles do not overlap and $E \cap O = \varnothing$.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 8 with two separate circles that do not touch: E holds 2, 4, 6 and O holds 1, 3, 5. The numbers 7 and 8 lie outside both. No number is in both circles.
visual.caption: Disjoint sets: $E \cap O = \varnothing$.

slides.narration: Sometimes two sets share nothing. The even numbers two, four, six and the odd numbers one, three, five are an example. Their circles do not touch, and their intersection is the empty set. Disjoint sets are important in counting, because the size of the union is then simply the sum of the two sizes.

slides.heading: Difference
slides.body_md: $A - B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \notin B\}$. Note $A - B \ne B - A$ in general.

visual.alt: A Venn diagram of U equal to 1 to 10 with two overlapping circles: P holds the primes 2, 3, 5, 7 and O holds the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Only P has 2; the overlap has 3, 5, 7; only O has 1 and 9; 4, 6, 8, 10 lie outside both.
visual.caption: Primes $P$ and odd numbers $O$ in $U = \{1, \dots, 10\}$.

slides.narration: The difference of A and B keeps the elements of A that are not in B. With P for primes and O for odd numbers, P minus O is just the number two, the only even prime. O minus P is one and nine. The order matters: the two differences are different sets, one on each side of the overlap.

slides.heading: Complement
slides.body_md: $A' = U - A$: everything in $U$ that is **not** in $A$. Then $A \cup A' = U$ and $A \cap A' = \varnothing$.

visual.alt: A rectangle U holding 1 to 10 with a circle P around the primes 2, 3, 5, 7. The complement of P is everything in the rectangle outside the circle: 1, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10.
visual.caption: The complement $P' = U - P$ is everything outside the circle.

slides.narration: The complement of a set is everything in the universal set that is outside it. It always depends on the universal set you chose. For the primes in the numbers one to ten, the complement is one, four, six, eight, nine and ten. A set and its complement together make the whole universal set and have nothing in common.

slides.heading: Quick check: a complement
slides.body_md: How many tickets were not for the evening show?
slides.narration: The universal set is all the tickets sold. Subtract the evening tickets.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: six operations
slides.body_md: For $U = \{1, \dots, 10\}$, $P$ = primes and $O$ = odd numbers, find $P \cup O$, $P \cap O$, $P - O$, $O - P$, $P'$ and $(P \cup O)'$.
bullets: Union: all elements of either set
Complements: from the numbers outside the circles

visual.alt: Table of six operations on the prime set P and the odd set O inside U of 1 to 10: union has 6 elements, intersection has 3, P minus O has 1, O minus P has 2, the complement of P has 6, and the complement of the union has 4.
visual.caption: All six results, listed from the diagram.

slides.narration: Work from the diagram. The union lists one, two, three, five, seven and nine. The intersection is three, five, seven. The two differences are two on one side and one and nine on the other. The complement of the primes has six elements, and the complement of the union is four, six, eight and ten. Every result is read straight from a region.

slides.heading: Laws of set algebra
slides.body_md: Union and intersection are **commutative** and **associative**, and each **distributes** over the other. Identity and complement laws hold. The table was checked on every triple of subsets of a four-element set.

headers: Checked on all $16^3$ triples of subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$

visual.alt: Table of nine laws of set algebra: commutative, associative, two distributive laws, two De Morgan laws, identity and complement, each with a tick showing it was checked on every triple of subsets of 1, 2, 3, 4.
visual.caption: Every law was verified by brute force.

slides.narration: Set operations obey laws much like those for numbers. Union and intersection can be swapped, regrouped, and each distributes over the other. There are also identity laws with the empty set and the universal set, and complement laws. The table lists nine laws, and each was verified by checking every possible triple of subsets of a four-element set.

slides.heading: De Morgan's laws
slides.body_md: $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$. Complement flips union and intersection.

visual.alt: Table of the four regions of a two-circle Venn diagram. Only the region outside both circles lies in the complement of the union, and only that region lies in both P-complement and O-complement, so the two sets are equal.
visual.caption: The last two columns agree in every row: De Morgan.

slides.narration: De Morgan laws tell you how a complement passes through a union or an intersection. Not in A or B means not in A and not in B. The table checks the four regions of a two-circle diagram. Only the region outside both circles belongs to the complement of the union, and only that region belongs to both complements. So the two sets are the same.

slides.heading: Quick check: De Morgan
slides.body_md: Pick the set equal to the complement of a union.
slides.narration: Recall that a complement flips the operation, so a union becomes an intersection of complements.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: verify a law

visual.alt: Table verifying one De Morgan law: the union of A and B is 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9; its complement is 1, 5, 7; and the intersection of the two complements is also 1, 5, 7.
visual.caption: Both sides give the same set.

slides.narration: To verify a law with numbers, compute each side separately and compare. The union of A and B has six elements, and its complement in one to nine is one, five, seven. The complements of A and B each have more elements, but their intersection is again one, five, seven. The two sides agree, as the law predicts.

slides.narration: Operations work on intervals too. Take minus three to two, excluding two, and zero to five, excluding zero. The intersection is zero to two, with both ends open, because zero is not in B and two is not in A. The union runs from minus three to five with both ends closed. The difference A minus B is minus three up to zero, including zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: interval end points
slides.body_md: For the intervals above, find $A \cap B$, $A \cup B$ and $A - B$.

visual.alt: Table of the three interval results with their end points: the intersection from 0 to 2 has both ends excluded, the union from minus 3 to 5 has both ends included, and the difference from minus 3 to 0 has both ends included.
visual.caption: Decide each end point by testing it in both sets.

slides.narration: The method is always the same. Find the end points, then test each one in both sets. Zero is not in B, so it cannot be in the intersection. Two is not in A, so the intersection excludes it too. For the union, minus three is in A and five is in B, so both stay. For the difference, zero is in A and not in B, so it stays.

slides.body_md: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Also $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$ and $n(A') = n(U) - n(A)$. **Formative only:** practical problems of this type are not board assessed.

In this example, among one hundred and twenty members, seventy use one app and fifty-five the other, with twenty-five using both. The diagram shows the four region counts, which add up to the total. These practical problems are for classroom practice and are not board assessed.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a word problem
slides.body_md: $120$ members: $70$ use app $A$, $55$ use app $B$, $25$ use both. How many use at least one, only $A$, neither?

slides.narration: Start with the union formula: seventy plus fifty-five minus twenty-five gives one hundred members who use at least one app. Only the first app is seventy minus the overlap, forty-five. Those who use neither are the complement of the union: one hundred twenty minus one hundred, twenty. The diagram confirms all four regions.

slides.heading: Counting three sets
slides.body_md: $n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(A \cap C) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$. Fill the Venn regions from the centre outwards.

For counting, add the sizes and subtract the overlap, and for three sets add back the triple overlap at the end.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Verify a law (2–3 marks):** compute both sides separately, then state they are equal
**Proof of an identity (3–5 marks):** two inclusions with a general element $x$
**Interval answers:** one mark per correct end-point decision
**Mistake:** subtracting the overlap twice, or not at all, in $n(A \cup B)$
**Mistake:** complement taken in the wrong universal set
slides.narration: In board-style answers, verification questions give a mark for each side computed and one for the conclusion. Proofs of identities need both inclusions, written with a general element. Interval answers are marked end point by end point. Common slips are swapping the two differences, miscounting the overlap in the union formula, and taking a complement in the wrong universal set.

sections.heading: 1. Sets and their representations
sections.body_md:
A **set** is a well-defined collection of objects; the objects are its **elements**. $a \in A$ means $a$ belongs to $A$.

- **Roster form:** list the elements once each, e.g. $\{7, 14, 21, 28, 35\}$.
- **Set-builder form:** give a rule, e.g. $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a multiple of } 7,\ x < 40\}$.

Standard sets: $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{W}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, each inside the next. For a set-builder rule, solve the condition inside the stated universe (negative integers count in $\mathbb{Z}$).

key_terms.definition_md: A well-defined collection: a clear rule settles membership.
An object in a set; $a \in A$.
The set written by listing its elements.
The set written by a rule its elements satisfy.

rows: $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \text{ is a multiple of } 7,\ x < 40\}$

sections.heading: 2. Types of sets and equal sets
sections.body_md:
- **Empty set** $\varnothing$: no element. $\{\varnothing\}$ is **not** empty; it has one element.
- **Singleton:** exactly one element.
- **Finite:** counting ends; $n(A)$ is the number of elements.
- **Infinite:** counting never ends.
- **Equal sets:** exactly the same elements. Order and repeats do not matter. Equal counts do not make equal sets.

To show $A = B$, show $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$.

key_terms.definition_md: A set whose elements can be counted to the end.
Sets with exactly the same elements.

formulas.latex: A = B \iff A \subseteq B \text{ and } B \subseteq A

sections.heading: 3. Subsets, power set and universal set
sections.body_md:
$B \subseteq A$ if every element of $B$ is in $A$; $B \subset A$ if also $B \ne A$ (**proper** subset). $\varnothing \subseteq A$ and $A \subseteq A$ always.

The **power set** $P(A)$ is the set of all subsets. If $n(A) = n$: subsets $2^n$; proper subsets $2^n - 1$; non-empty proper subsets $2^n - 2$. Fixing $k$ elements inside leaves $2^{n-k}$ subsets.

The **universal set** $U$ contains every set of the discussion; it is the rectangle of a Venn diagram.

key_terms.definition_md: $B \subseteq A$: every element of $B$ is in $A$.
$P(A)$: the set of all subsets of $A$.
The set $U$ of which all sets under discussion are subsets.

sections.heading: 4. Intervals
sections.body_md:
Intervals are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. $(a, b)$ excludes both ends; $[a, b]$ includes both; $[a, b)$ and $(a, b]$ include one. $(a, \infty)$ and $(-\infty, b]$ are unbounded. $\infty$ is never included.

On the number line: filled circle = included, open circle = excluded.

Integers in an interval: count the end points carefully. $(-2, 3)$ has $4$, $[-2, 3]$ has $6$, $[-2, 3)$ has $5$.

key_terms.definition_md: $[a, b)$ or $(a, b]$: one end included.

sections.heading: 5. Venn diagrams and operations
sections.body_md:
- **Union** $A \cup B$: in $A$ or $B$ (or both).
- **Intersection** $A \cap B$: in both. **Disjoint** if $A \cap B = \varnothing$.
- **Difference** $A - B$: in $A$, not in $B$. In general $A - B \ne B - A$.
- **Complement** $A' = U - A$.

In a Venn diagram, label the regions: only $A$, both, only $B$, outside. For intervals, test every end point in both sets: $[-3, 2) \cap (0, 5] = (0, 2)$, $[-3, 2) \cup (0, 5] = [-3, 5]$.

key_terms.definition_md: All elements of either set, each listed once.
The elements common to both sets.
$A' = U - A$, the elements of $U$ not in $A$.

sections.heading: 6. Laws of set algebra
sections.body_md:
- **Commutative:** $A \cup B = B \cup A$, $A \cap B = B \cap A$.
- **Associative:** $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$, and the same for $\cap$.
- **Distributive:** $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$, $A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$.
- **De Morgan:** $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$, $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$.
- **Identity / complement:** $A \cup \varnothing = A$, $A \cap U = A$, $A \cup A' = U$, $A \cap A' = \varnothing$.

To **verify** a law, compute both sides for the given sets. To **prove** an identity, show each side is a subset of the other using a general element $x$.

**How marks are awarded**
- *Roster / set-builder (1–2 marks):* solve the condition, list each element once.
- *Subset counts (1–2 marks):* $2^n$ with the reason.
- *Verify a law (2–3 marks):* each side computed separately 1 + 1, conclusion 1.
- *Prove an identity (3–5 marks):* each inclusion with a general $x$, then the conclusion.
- *Intervals (2–5 marks):* one mark per correct end-point decision.
- *Word problems (2–5 marks):* formula or Venn diagram 1, each region or total 1.

**Common mistakes**
1. Calling $\{\varnothing\}$ the empty set.
2. Leaving out negative integers or $0$ when the universe is $\mathbb{Z}$.
3. Treating $A - B$ as $B - A$.
4. Writing a square bracket next to $\infty$.
5. Counting the overlap twice in $n(A \cup B)$.
6. Taking a complement in the wrong universal set.
7. Proving a set identity with one example instead of a general element.
8. Mathematical Induction is formative only and Mathematical Reasoning is deleted: neither is examined here.

questions.stem_md: Which of these collections is well defined, and so forms a set?

options.text_md: The cleverest pupils of a Class 11 section
The most beautiful rivers of India
The tastiest street snacks of Lucknow

questions.solution_md: A set needs a clear rule that decides membership. "Prime and between $20$ and $40$" does: $23, 29, 31, 37$. "Tastiest", "cleverest" and "most beautiful" depend on opinion.

questions.stem_md: In roster form, the set $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \text{ is odd and } x^2 < 20\}$ is
questions.solution_md: Odd integers with $x^2 < 20$ need $|x| \le 4$, so $x = \pm 1, \pm 3$. Negative integers belong to $\mathbb{Z}$ too, and $x = \pm 5$ gives $25 > 20$.

questions.stem_md: How many elements does $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : -3 \le 2x + 1 < 9\}$ have?
questions.solution_md: $-3 \le 2x + 1 < 9$ gives $-4 \le 2x < 8$, so $-2 \le x < 4$. The integers are $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3$: $6$ elements.

questions.stem_md: Which of these sets has no element at all?
questions.solution_md: $x^2 + 4 \ge 4 > 0$ for every real $x$, so the first set is empty. The others hold $\pm 4$, $\dfrac25$ and $1$ respectively.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of sets is equal?
questions.solution_md: $x^2 - 7x + 12 = (x - 3)(x - 4)$ has roots $3$ and $4$, and repeating $4$ does not change a set. The other pairs differ: $\{1, 2\}$ against $\{1, 2, 3\}$; $\{-3, 3\}$ against $\{3\}$; one element against none.

questions.stem_md: A set has $5$ elements. How many of its subsets are non-empty and proper?
questions.solution_md: A $5$-element set has $2^5 = 32$ subsets. Remove the empty set and the set itself: $32 - 2 = 30$.

questions.stem_md: For $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$, which statement is correct?
questions.solution_md: Every element of $\{1, 2\}$ lies in $A$, so $\{1, 2\} \subset A$. The set $\{1, 2\}$ is not itself an element of $A$; $2$ is an element, not a subset; and $\varnothing$ is a subset of $A$, not an element.

questions.stem_md: The interval $[-1, 4)$ is the same set as
questions.solution_md: The square bracket at $-1$ means $-1$ is included ($-1 \le x$); the round bracket at $4$ means $4$ is excluded ($x < 4$).

questions.stem_md: How many integers belong to the interval $(-2, 3]$?
questions.solution_md: $-2$ is excluded and $3$ is included, so the integers are $-1, 0, 1, 2, 3$: five of them. (Counting $-2$ as well would give $6$.)

questions.stem_md: Roll numbers $1$ to $40$ are listed. $A$ holds the roll numbers divisible by $4$ and $B$ those divisible by $6$. Then $n(A \cap B)$ equals
questions.solution_md: A number divisible by both $4$ and $6$ is a multiple of their least common multiple $12$: $12, 24, 36$. So $n(A \cap B) = 3$. The values $6$, $10$ and $13$ are $n(B)$, $n(A)$ and $n(A \cup B)$.

questions.stem_md: $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 12\}$, $A$ is the set of even numbers in $U$ and $B$ the set of multiples of $3$ in $U$. The set $A - B$ is
questions.solution_md: $A - B$ keeps the even numbers that are not multiples of $3$: $2, 4, 8, 10$. The other sets are $A \cap B$, $B - A$ and the elements in exactly one of the two sets.

questions.stem_md: The universal set is $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 15\}$ and $A$ is the set of primes in $U$. Then $n(A')$ equals
questions.solution_md: $A = \{2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13\}$ has $6$ elements, so $n(A') = 15 - 6 = 9$ (the number $1$ is not prime and belongs to $A'$). Counting only composites would give $8$.

questions.stem_md: In a Class 11 section, $18$ students take Economics ($A$), $14$ take Accountancy ($B$) and $5$ take both. The number taking at least one of the two is
questions.solution_md: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B) = 18 + 14 - 5 = 27$. Adding without subtracting counts the $5$ students twice and gives $32$.

questions.stem_md: A theatre sold $60$ tickets, and $38$ of them were for the evening show. How many tickets were not for the evening show?
questions.solution_md: With $U$ the $60$ tickets and $A$ the evening tickets, $n(A') = n(U) - n(A) = 60 - 38 = 22$.

questions.stem_md: De Morgan's law for union: the set $(A \cup B)'$ is equal to
questions.solution_md: An element outside $A \cup B$ is outside $A$ and outside $B$, i.e. in $A' \cap B'$. The set $A' \cup B'$ equals $(A \cap B)'$, the other De Morgan law.

questions.stem_md: The distributive law for sets states that $A \cap (B \cup C)$ is equal to
questions.solution_md: Intersection distributes over union: an element of $A$ that lies in $B$ or in $C$ lies in $A \cap B$ or in $A \cap C$. Option $(A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$ equals $A \cup (B \cap C)$, the other distributive law.

questions.stem_md: Of the $35$ volunteers in a clean-up drive ($A$), $12$ also joined the tree-planting team ($B$). The number who joined only the clean-up drive is
questions.solution_md: Only the clean-up drive means $A - B$: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B) = 35 - 12 = 23$.

questions.stem_md: How many sets $X$ satisfy $\{1, 2\} \subseteq X \subseteq \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$?
questions.solution_md: $X$ must contain $1$ and $2$; each of the other four elements $3, 4, 5, 6$ may be in or out: $2^4 = 16$ sets. Allowing all six to vary would give $2^6 = 64$, and fixing only one of $1, 2$ gives $32$.

questions.stem_md: If $A = (-3, 2]$ and $B = [0, 5)$ are intervals on the real line, then $A \cap B$ is
questions.solution_md: The overlap starts at $0$, which is in $B$ and also in $A$ (since $-3 < 0 \le 2$), and ends at $2$, which is in $A$ and in $B$ (since $0 \le 2 < 5$). So both end points belong: $[0, 2]$.

questions.stem_md: If $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$ for two sets $A$ and $B$, then
questions.solution_md: Each set is contained in the other, so they have exactly the same elements: $A = B$. This is how equality of two sets is proved.

**Assertion (A):** The intersection $[1, 3] \cap [3, 5]$ is the single-element set $\{3\}$.

**Reason (R):** The intersection of two sets is a subset of each of the two sets.

**Assertion (A):** For any two sets $A$ and $B$, the sets $A - B$ and $A \cap B$ have no element in common.

**Reason (R):** Every element of $A - B$ is outside $B$, while every element of $A \cap B$ is inside $B$.

**Assertion (A):** If $A \subseteq B$, then $A \cup B = B$.

**Reason (R):** If $A \subseteq B$, then $A \cap B = B$.

questions.solution_md: A is true: nothing in $A$ adds a new element to $B$. R is false: when $A \subseteq B$ the common part is $A$, so $A \cap B = A$ (for example $A = \{1\}$, $B = \{1, 2\}$ gives $A \cap B = \{1\}$, not $B$).

questions.stem_md: The set $\{\varnothing\}$ has no element, so it is the empty set.
questions.solution_md: $\{\varnothing\}$ has exactly one element, namely $\varnothing$. It is a box holding an empty box, not an empty set.

questions.stem_md: The interval $(2, 5]$ is a subset of the interval $[2, 5]$.
questions.solution_md: Every number with $2 < x \le 5$ also satisfies $2 \le x \le 5$. (The converse fails: $2$ is in $[2, 5]$ but not in $(2, 5]$.)

questions.stem_md: If two finite sets $A$ and $B$ satisfy $n(A) = n(B)$, then $A = B$.
questions.solution_md: Equal sets have the same elements, not merely the same count: $\{a, b\}$ and $\{c, d\}$ both have $2$ elements but are different sets.

questions.stem_md: The union of the intervals $[1, 2]$ and $(2, 3]$ is the interval $[1, 3]$.
questions.solution_md: The first interval covers $1 \le x \le 2$ and the second covers $2 < x \le 3$. Together they cover $1 \le x \le 3$ with no gap, because $2$ is already in the first.

questions.stem_md: For any two sets $A$ and $B$, the set $A \cap B$ is always a subset of $A \cup B$.
questions.solution_md: An element of $A \cap B$ is in $A$, and so it is in $A \cup B$.

questions.stem_md: The power set of the empty set is the empty set.
questions.solution_md: The empty set has one subset, namely itself, so its power set is $\{\varnothing\}$ with $2^0 = 1$ element, which is not empty.

questions.stem_md: A set with $6$ elements has exactly ____ subsets.
questions.solution_md: Each element is either in a subset or out of it: $2^6 = 64$.

questions.stem_md: The collection of all subsets of a set $A$ is called the ____ set of $A$.
questions.solution_md: It is written $P(A)$ and called the power set of $A$.

questions.stem_md: If $A$ is a subset of the universal set $U$, then $A \cup A'$ equals ____.
questions.solution_md: Every element of $U$ is either in $A$ or in $A'$, so $A \cup A' = U$.

questions.stem_md: How many subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ contain both $3$ and $5$?
questions.solution_md: A subset containing $3$ and $5$ is decided by the other three elements $1, 2, 4$, each in or out: $2^3 = 8$.

questions.solution_md: $|x - 2| \le 3$ means $-3 \le x - 2 \le 3$, so $-1 \le x \le 5$. The integers $-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ give $7$ elements; the count is $5 - (-1) + 1 = 7$.

questions.solution_md: The overlap is $[0, 4]$, because $0$ is in both and $4$ is in both. Its integers are $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$: $5$ of them.

Write the set $A = \{x \in \mathbb{N} : x^2 < 50 \text{ and } x \text{ is odd}\}$ in roster form, and write the set $B$ of distinct letters of the word MISSISSIPPI with its number of elements.

answer.model_answer_md:

$B$: the distinct letters are $M, I, S, P$, so $B = \{I, M, P, S\}$ and $n(B) = 4$.

questions.stem_md: Write the set $\{2, 5, 8, 11, 14\}$ in set-builder form, using a rule in $n$ and a condition on $n$. Then state whether the set is finite or infinite.

answer.model_answer_md: Each element is one less than a multiple of $3$: $3 \cdot 1 - 1 = 2$, $3 \cdot 2 - 1 = 5$, and so on up to $3 \cdot 5 - 1 = 14$. So the set is $\{3n - 1 : n \in \mathbb{N},\ n \le 5\}$. It has $5$ elements, so it is finite.

questions.stem_md: Classify each set as empty, finite non-empty or infinite: (i) $\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x < 1\}$; (ii) $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x^2 = 9\}$; (iii) $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : 1 < x < 2\}$.

(iii) Between $1$ and $2$ lie $1.1, 1.01, 1.001, \dots$ and endlessly many more: infinite.

questions.stem_md:
A survey of $200$ families in a housing colony found that $130$ buy a newspaper ($N$), $95$ buy a magazine ($M$) and $40$ buy neither.

(a) How many families buy at least one of the two?

(b) How many buy both?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Neither: $40$, so at least one: $200 - 40 = 160$.

Check: $65 + 65 + 30 + 40 = 200$.

questions.stem_md: For the real intervals $A = (-2, 5]$ and $B = [1, 9)$, find $A \cup B$, $A \cap B$, $A - B$, $B - A$ and the complement $A'$ in $\mathbb{R}$. Show the end-point decisions.

answer.model_answer_md:
$A \cup B$: the intervals overlap, so there is no gap. The left end $-2$ is not in $A$ or $B$, the right end $9$ is not in $B$: $(-2, 9)$.

$A \cap B$: starts at $1$ (in $B$ and in $A$) and ends at $5$ (in $A$ and in $B$): $[1, 5]$.

$A - B$: the part of $A$ left of $B$; $1$ is in $B$, so it is removed: $(-2, 1)$.

$B - A$: the part of $B$ right of $A$; $5$ is in $A$, so it is removed: $(5, 9)$.

$A'$: everything outside $(-2, 5]$; $-2$ is outside $A$ and $5$ is inside: $(-\infty, -2] \cup (5, \infty)$.
